panels.description: Number of pipeline components currently exerting backpressure (i.e. signalling they are not ready to accept more work). Any non-zero value means the pipeline is throttled somewhere. Check the Backpressure History timeline and Current Backpressure Causes table below to identify the source.
panels.title: Active Backpressure Causes

panels.description: The highest output-channel queue depth across all pipeline components. A growing queue means the downstream consumer of that channel is processing slower than the upstream producer — sustained growth leads to backpressure. Drill into Queue Depth By Component to identify which component.
panels.title: Worst Queue Depth

panels.description: The largest number of blocks any single component is behind the pipeline head. Zero means all components are processing the latest block. Rising lag in a specific component means it cannot keep up with block production — use Block Lag By Component to identify which one.
panels.title: Worst Block Lag

panels.description: Wall-clock seconds between the block timestamp of the pipeline head and the most recently processed block of the slowest component. Unlike block lag, this accounts for block timing variance and reflects real delay from the user's perspective. Yellow ≥ 5s, Red ≥ 30s. Returns 0 if timestamp is unavailable.
panels.title: Worst Time Lag

panels.description: Peak block processing rate across all components (blocks per second).
panels.title: Peak Throughput (blocks/s)

panels.description: Green = no backpressure anywhere. Red = at least one component is under backpressure.
panels.title: Overall Pipeline Health

panels.description: Components whose backpressure signal is currently active (pipeline_backpressure_active = 1). An empty table means the pipeline is flowing freely. Multiple rows indicate a cascade — the root cause is typically the deepest upstream component in the list, not the last one to appear.
panels.title: Current Backpressure Causes

panels.description: Count of transitions into backpressure ('opened') and out of backpressure ('cleared') per scrape interval. Frequent oscillation (high open+cleared rate) means the pipeline is on the edge of stability — a component is repeatedly hitting its capacity limit. A sustained 'opened' count with no matching 'cleared' means a component is stuck.
panels.title: Acceptance State Transitions

panels.description: Shows which components were in active backpressure over time. Red = backpressure active.

Swimlane view of backpressure state per component over time. Green = accepting work normally, Red = backpressure active. Use this during incidents to find which component went red first and trace the cascade. The first component to turn red is usually the root cause; others follow downstream.
panels.title: Backpressure History by Component

panels.description: Output channel queue depth for every pipeline component over time. Zero depth means the downstream consumer is keeping up. A component whose queue grows while others stay near zero is the bottleneck. Spikes that self-resolve indicate burst load; a queue that never drains means the component is saturated.
panels.title: Queue Depth By Component

panels.description: How many blocks behind the pipeline head each component currently is. All lines should track close together near zero. Diverging lines mean one component has stalled. The component with the highest lag is the current bottleneck.
panels.title: Block Lag By Component

panels.description: Difference in seconds between the wall-clock timestamp of the latest produced block and the timestamp embedded in the last block each component processed. Complements block lag by accounting for variable block times — a component 10 blocks behind during fast block production may only be 2s behind in real time. Returns 0 if the component or pipeline head has no timestamp.
panels.title: Time Lag By Component

panels.description: Block processing rate per component. A drop here indicates a stalling component before lag metrics climb.
panels.title: Processing Throughput By Component (blocks/s)

panels.description: Absolute block number of the last block successfully processed by each component. All lines should advance together at roughly the same slope. A flat line for one component means it has stopped making progress. Useful for post-incident analysis: zoom into the window where lines diverged to pinpoint the exact moment a component stalled.
panels.title: Last Processed Block By Component

panels.description: Output channel queue depth for the sequencer execution path: block_executor → block_canonizer → block_applier → tree_manager. Queues in block_applier or tree_manager (which write to storage and the Merkle tree) typically indicate I/O saturation rather than CPU pressure.
panels.title: Sequencer Path Queue Depth

panels.description: Output channel queue depth for the proving path: prover_input_generator → batcher → batch_verification → fri_job_manager → snark_job_manager → gapless_committer → gapless_l1_proof_sender. Some queue depth here is normal since proving is slower than block production — watch for unbounded monotonic growth which signals the prover is falling permanently behind.
panels.title: Prover Path Queue Depth

panels.description: Output channel queue depth for L1 settlement components: l1_sender_commit, l1_sender_prove, l1_sender_execute, priority_tree. Growth here usually indicates L1 submission is congested — check gas prices, nonce sequencing issues, or operator ETH balance running low.
panels.title: Settlement Path Queue Depth

panels.description: Block lag for the sequencer execution path components: block_executor, block_canonizer, block_applier, tree_manager. These should all stay near zero. A lag spike in tree_manager while block_applier is fine suggests Merkle tree computation is the bottleneck.
panels.title: Sequencer Path Block Lag

panels.description: Block lag for the proving path components: prover_input_generator, batcher, batch_verification, fri_job_manager, snark_job_manager, gapless_committer, gapless_l1_proof_sender. A steadily growing lag here is expected if the proof pipeline is slower than block production — alert only if the rate of growth accelerates.
panels.title: Prover Path Block Lag

panels.description: Block lag for L1 settlement components: l1_sender_commit, l1_sender_prove, l1_sender_execute, priority_tree. These lag behind the prover path by design. A sudden increase compared to the prover path lag suggests an L1 submission issue rather than a sequencing issue.
panels.title: Settlement Path Block Lag

panels.description: Wall-clock time lag for sequencer path components (block_executor, block_canonizer, block_applier, tree_manager). Should stay near zero in normal operation. A rising value here directly translates to delayed transaction finality visible to users.
panels.title: Sequencer Path Time Lag

panels.description: Wall-clock time lag for the proving path components. A baseline lag is expected since proof generation takes longer than block production. What matters is whether this lag is stable (acceptable) or growing over time (prover falling behind permanently).
panels.title: Prover Path Time Lag

panels.description: Wall-clock time lag for L1 settlement components (l1_sender_commit, l1_sender_prove, l1_sender_execute, priority_tree). This represents how far behind on-chain state is from the latest sequenced blocks. Compare to the proving path time lag — if settlement lag grows faster than prover lag, the bottleneck is specifically in L1 submission.
panels.title: Settlement Path Time Lag

panels.description: Fraction of time each component spends in each generic state (working, waiting, idle, etc.). Stacked = 100% of time. A wide 'waiting' band points to upstream stall; a wide 'idle' band points to empty queue.
panels.title: Component Time Distribution by State (stacked %)

panels.description: Absolute seconds per second each component spends in each specific state. Useful for spotting which sub-state is consuming the most wall time.
panels.title: Component Time By Specific State (absolute s/s)

panels.description: Absolute rate (seconds per second) of time each component accumulates in each generic state. Values for a single component should sum to ~1.0. Useful alongside the stacked % view above when you want to compare absolute magnitudes across components — e.g. two components both spending 50% in 'waiting' but one has 10× higher absolute rate indicates very different workloads.
panels.title: Component State Time Rate

panels.description: Number of L1 transactions currently in-flight simultaneously per sender command (parallel_transactions), and the current nonce (nonce). High parallelism with a stalled nonce means transactions are stuck waiting for confirmation — check gas price or network congestion. A nonce that never advances means no transactions are landing on L1.
panels.title: L1 Sender Parallelism And Nonce

panels.description: ETH balance of the operator wallet used by each L1 sender (commit/prove/execute). A declining balance is normal — gas is being spent. Alert before it approaches zero: when the wallet runs dry the sender stops submitting transactions entirely, causing settlement lag to spike. The legend shows the minimum observed balance in the selected time range.
panels.title: L1 Sender Operator Balance
